author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Space Between Songs
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The pier reopened on a day when the wind couldn't decide what it wanted.

It blew warm from the sea in the morning, cold from the ridge by noon, and sideways through the lantern hooks just as Greg arrived with his guitar. The volunteer crew had spent the previous week finishing the western boardwalk repairs and checking every railing under the load limits Tamsin had approved.

Edda had tested the path.

Danse had checked the fasteners.

Toph had listened to the stone supports beneath the timbers.

Fen had signed the tide schedule.

The reopening could have been a grand celebration.

Greg asked for a small concert.

"Just a few songs," he said. "No big announcement."

I looked at him.

"Are you sure?"

"Yeah. I want to play because I want to play."

That was a good enough reason.

We arranged the chairs in a half-circle beside the safe stage. The accessible path remained open. The west railing had a new maintenance marker, and the old closed sign was stored where it could be used again if future inspections required it.

Nothing was being declared safe forever.

The work had simply reached the point where people could use the space again.

At sunset, Greg took the stage.

He looked out at the small gathering: Mara with a basket of bread, Iroh holding two cups of tea, Toph seated near a support where she could feel the rhythm, Danse standing beside the repaired railing, and Maui helping a child hang a paper fish where the wind wouldn't tear it away.

Steven was there too.

He had arrived through the Starwake Door earlier that afternoon, carrying a small bag of snacks and looking pleased to see his father doing something that belonged to him.

"Hey, Dad," he'd said, hugging Greg.

"Hey, buddy."

Steven looked at the guitar.

"New song?"

"Couple of them."

"Cool."

No interrogation. No demand that Greg perform grief or explain his relationship with Jasper. Just a son showing up because he wanted to hear his dad play.

I sat near the front.

Greg looked at me, grinned, and lifted the guitar.

"This first one is about a chair," he said.

Toph groaned.

"Of course it is."

The crowd laughed.

He played the melody he'd begun after the Listening Fair, the one with space between the phrases. The repaired guitar sounded different from before, warmer on one low note. Greg didn't hide it. He let the new sound become part of the song.

The next piece was about coming back to a place that had changed. He'd written it after building the bench at Tideglass with Maui and Ilya. It wasn't a song about being the hero of the story. It was about the little ferry bell that told people when the upper path was open.

I looked toward Maui.

He smiled.

The final song was new.

Greg didn't introduce it with a speech. He simply played, and the notes moved through the evening air like lantern light on water. There were spaces where I could hear the sea. There were moments when the melody almost stopped, then found another way to continue.

I felt tears gather unexpectedly.

Not because it was sad.

Because it sounded like the life we'd built.

When the last note faded, the crowd applauded. Greg smiled, bowed awkwardly, and put the guitar away before anybody could ask for a song he didn't want to play.

The concert was over.

The evening wasn't.

We shared bread and tea, helped collect the chairs, and made sure the volunteers who had agreed to clean up were actually relieved when their shifts ended. Steven helped carry the snack table back to storage. Maui asked Greg about the low note in the repaired guitar, and Danse explained the bridge repair without turning it into a lecture.

Toph told all three men they were becoming unbearable.

They laughed.

Later, when the pier was quiet, Greg and I sat on the safe bench by the railing. The lights from Lanternwell reflected across the water.

"Well?" he asked.

"Well what?"

"Was it worth the trouble?"

I looked at the repaired boards.

"Every argument about load limits and chair placement?"

"Especially those."

"Yes."

He smiled.

I leaned against him.

"You didn't play the old song," I said.

"No."

"Do you wish you had?"

He shook his head.

"I played what I wanted."

I took his hand.

"Good."

For a while we listened to the water moving beneath the pier. The strange low note didn't sound tonight. Fen's tide chart showed ordinary conditions, and the repaired supports had passed their tests.

That didn't mean the old drainage mystery was over.

It meant we'd learned how to keep the pier safe while the larger investigation continued.

The next afternoon, Nola came to check the storage shed before the public key policy was finalized. The building belonged to the community, and Greg couldn't simply hand out permanent access because he was fond of somebody.

"There's a visitor-use key," she explained. "People can borrow it for the quiet room and return it to the desk. The instrument cupboard stays locked unless a staff member opens it."

Greg looked sheepish. "I was going to give Jasper a key."

"You can give Jasper an invitation," Nola said. "That might be enough."

I appreciated that she didn't say it to embarrass him. She was protecting the instruments other musicians had lent, the tools workers needed, and the room anyone could request without having to know Greg personally.

"Could I still come sit by the water?" I asked.

"Of course. There's a sign-up book for the room, not a membership test. You can choose whether to give a contact number for emergency closures. We don't publish who's there."

Greg glanced at me. "Would you like to use the visitor key?"

"I would."

He looked pleased enough that I wanted to kiss him. I held off until Nola went back to the desk, then asked whether he minded.

"Mind? I have been practicing my casual romantic expression all afternoon."

It was a terrible expression. I laughed and kissed him anyway.

For a moment, the music and the public work fell away. His fingers rested lightly against my cheek; I could smell salt on his jacket and the faint sweetness of the lemonade we'd shared at the concert. Then he stepped back, careful not to make the kiss an answer to a question I hadn't asked.

"I like that you can come here even when I don't," he said.

"Me too. I have other people to visit, and other things I want to do. But I want this to be a place I return to."

He nodded. "That sounds like home."

"One kind of home."

"Yeah. One kind."

I thought about all the versions of belonging we'd argued over: a stage, a van, a small town, a valley where visitors could leave. None of them required one person to own the door. The chance to return mattered because the chance to go was real.

We took the shed's posted access rules back to Nola and asked her to confirm the dates for the next sound check. The concert was over. The responsibility to keep the place useful wasn't.

Greg turned toward me.

"Do you want a key?" he asked.

I blinked.

"To what?"

"The storage shed. Not because you have to help. Just so you can come here when you want to sit by the water."

I looked at him.

"Are you sure?"

"Yeah. You've got a life in a lot of places. I like that this can be one of them."

I smiled.

"Then yes."

He placed the little key in my hand.

It was ordinary brass, with a paper tag showing the storage shed's number and the rules for borrowing equipment.

No destiny.

No ownership.

Just trust, with instructions attached.

I laughed.

"Very romantic."

"I try."

He kissed me, gentle and warm, then rested his forehead against mine.

"Love you," he whispered.

"Love you too."

We stayed until the last lantern was turned down.

The next morning, the pier would need sweeping. The repair fund would need another entry. Greg would have a song to finish, and I would have appointments in other districts, with other people I loved.

None of that made tonight smaller.

When we stood to leave, Greg looked back at the empty stage.

"Should we leave the last chair out?"

"For whom?"

"Whoever comes next."

I considered the clear walkway, the weather forecast, and the storage rules.

"Inside by the door," I said. "Available, but not blocking the path."

He laughed.

"Practical romance."

"The best kind."

We carried the chair together.

At the Starwake Door, he paused and offered his hand.

I took it.

The space between songs was never empty.

It was where we chose to listen.
